en.title: Roorkee is home to Asia's oldest engineering institute
en.shortDescription: IIT Roorkee began in 1847 as Thomason College of Civil Engineering, making it the oldest engineering institution in Asia.
en.longDescription: Founded in 1847 as Thomason College of Civil Engineering, the institution here became a University of Roorkee in 1949 and was converted into an Indian Institute of Technology in 2001. It is widely cited as the oldest engineering institution in Asia.
en.narrationHint: The town on your right built engineers for over 175 years.

en.title: A canal crosses a river on a bridge near Roorkee
en.shortDescription: Near Roorkee, the Upper Ganga Canal is carried over the Solani river on a masonry aqueduct, an unusual 19th-century engineering solution.
en.longDescription: When British engineers built the Upper Ganga Canal in the 1850s, the alignment had to cross the Solani river. Rather than let the canal and river mix, they built the Solani Aqueduct, an elevated channel that carries canal water clean over the riverbed below.
en.narrationHint: Water flowing over water, not into it.

en.title: A Sufi shrine near Roorkee draws pilgrims of many faiths
en.shortDescription: The dargah of Sufi saint Alauddin Ali Ahmad Sabir Kaliyari at Kaliyar village near Roorkee hosts a major annual Urs fair.
en.longDescription: Kaliyar village, a short distance from Roorkee, is home to the dargah of 13th-century Sufi saint Alauddin Ali Ahmad Sabir Kaliyari. Its annual Urs fair draws large crowds of both Muslim and Hindu pilgrims, reflecting a long shared devotional tradition in this area.
en.narrationHint: A shrine nearby is visited across faith lines every year.

en.title: An evening Ganga Aarti has been performed at Har Ki Pauri for generations
en.shortDescription: Har Ki Pauri ghat in Haridwar hosts a daily evening Ganga Aarti, one of the most recognizable religious rituals on the river.
en.longDescription: Har Ki Pauri, meaning 'footsteps of the Lord', is Haridwar's most sacred ghat on the Ganges. Every evening at sunset, priests perform an Aarti with fire and flowers as crowds gather along the steps, a ritual that draws pilgrims and visitors year-round.
en.narrationHint: This ghat lights up with fire lamps every evening at sunset.

en.title: Haridwar is one of only four Kumbh Mela sites
en.shortDescription: The Kumbh Mela, one of the largest religious gatherings on earth, rotates between four cities in India, and Haridwar is one of them.
en.longDescription: The Kumbh Mela rotates roughly every 12 years between four sacred river locations: Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik, and Ujjain. Haridwar's turn draws millions of pilgrims to bathe in the Ganges at exactly this stretch of river.
en.narrationHint: Once every 12 years, millions gather right here.

en.title: A hilltop temple above Haridwar is reached by cable car
en.shortDescription: Chandi Devi Temple sits atop Neel Parvat hill overlooking Haridwar and is reachable by a ropeway.
en.longDescription: Chandi Devi Temple, built in the 17th century and expanded in the early 1900s, sits atop Neel Parvat hill on the eastern bank of the Ganges. It is considered one of the Siddh Peeths and is reached today by a ropeway that runs above the town.
en.narrationHint: A temple on the hill above town, reached by cable car.

en.title: The Ganges leaves the mountains at Rishikesh
en.shortDescription: Rishikesh sits at the exact point where the Ganges exits the Himalayan foothills and enters the plains.
en.longDescription: Rishikesh marks the transition point where the Ganges, after descending through the Himalayan foothills, reaches the plains of northern India. This geographic position is part of why the town has long been treated as a threshold between mountain pilgrimage routes and the plains below.
en.narrationHint: The river beside you just left the mountains behind.

en.title: Rishikesh calls itself the Yoga Capital of the World
en.shortDescription: Rishikesh has hosted yoga ashrams and teaching centers for over a century and is widely promoted as the world's yoga capital.
en.longDescription: Rishikesh has been a center for yoga instruction and ashram life since the early 20th century, with dozens of ashrams and yoga schools now operating along the river. The town markets itself internationally as the Yoga Capital of the World and hosts an annual International Yoga Festival.
en.narrationHint: This is the town that calls itself the world's yoga capital.

en.title: Lakshman Jhula replaced an earlier rope bridge
en.shortDescription: The iron suspension bridge at Lakshman Jhula was built in 1929 after an earlier rope bridge and a subsequent bridge were both washed away by floods.
en.longDescription: An early rope bridge at this crossing was destroyed by floods in 1924. It was replaced in 1929 by the iron suspension bridge that still stands today, a recognizable landmark connecting the two banks of the Ganges at Rishikesh. It was closed to vehicle and heavy foot traffic in 2024 due to structural concerns.
en.narrationHint: This bridge replaced one that floods washed away a century ago.

en.title: Swarg Ashram is a cluster of ashrams along the Ganges
en.shortDescription: The Swarg Ashram area near Ram Jhula is lined with ashrams, temples, and ghats that have drawn spiritual seekers for decades.
en.longDescription: Swarg Ashram, on the eastern bank near Ram Jhula, grew around a cluster of ashrams and temples in the early-to-mid 20th century. Pedestrian-only lanes here are lined with shops, temples, and meditation halls, and the area remains one of Rishikesh's main centers for spiritual visitors.
en.narrationHint: This riverside stretch has been an ashram town for decades.

en.title: The Beatles once studied meditation near here
en.shortDescription: In 1968 the Beatles spent weeks at Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's ashram near Rishikesh, an abandoned site now known as the Beatles Ashram.
en.longDescription: In February 1968, the Beatles traveled to Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's ashram near Rishikesh to study Transcendental Meditation, writing much of what became The White Album during their stay. The site was later abandoned, absorbed into forest department land, and reopened to visitors in 2015 as a heritage site nicknamed the Beatles Ashram, now known for its wall murals.
en.narrationHint: The Beatles wrote songs near here in 1968.

en.title: Rishikesh is the road gateway to the Char Dham pilgrimage
en.shortDescription: Road journeys to the Himalayan Char Dham shrines of Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath, and Badrinath typically begin from Rishikesh.
en.longDescription: Rishikesh serves as the main staging point for pilgrims traveling by road to the four Char Dham shrines in the Garhwal Himalayas: Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath, and Badrinath. Buses, taxis, and pilgrim convoys heading further into the mountains typically pass through or start from here.
en.narrationHint: Mountain pilgrimage routes to four shrines all start near here.

en.title: A restaurant mascot has marked this ghat for decades
en.shortDescription: Chotiwala, a pure-vegetarian restaurant near Har Ki Pauri, is fronted by a costumed doorman with a distinctive oversized topknot and has become a recognizable landmark on the ghat itself.
en.longDescription: Since the mid-20th century, a restaurant called Chotiwala near Har Ki Pauri has stationed a costumed figure with a painted face and an oversized topknot, or 'choti', outside its entrance. The mascot became so well known that a second, rival Chotiwala restaurant later opened nearby using the same character, and both remain fixtures of the ghat's food scene today.
en.narrationHint: Look for a costumed doorman with a giant topknot outside a restaurant near the ghat — that's Chotiwala.

en.title: Haridwar's food follows strict pilgrim-town rules
en.shortDescription: As a major pilgrimage site, Haridwar enforces a pure-vegetarian, satvik food culture — the sale of meat, eggs, and alcohol is prohibited within municipal limits.
en.longDescription: Haridwar's status as one of Hinduism's holiest river towns comes with civic food rules: the municipal area prohibits the sale of meat, eggs, and alcohol, and most eateries serve only satvik vegetarian food, often without onion or garlic, in keeping with pilgrim dietary traditions.
en.narrationHint: This town restricts what can legally be sold as food, right down to onion and garlic.

sourceName: Rishikesh municipal food regulations and yoga tourism history

en.title: Rishikesh sells no meat or alcohol within town limits
en.shortDescription: Like Haridwar upriver, Rishikesh prohibits the sale of meat and alcohol, and its food scene leans heavily toward vegetarian, Ayurvedic, and health-focused cafes catering to yoga travellers.
en.longDescription: Rishikesh's municipal limits ban the sale of meat and alcohol, a rule tied to its identity as a pilgrimage and yoga town. In recent decades this has combined with an influx of international yoga travellers to produce a distinctive cafe culture — vegetarian and vegan menus, Ayurvedic thalis, and health-food restaurants line the ghats alongside more traditional pilgrim food stalls.
en.narrationHint: No meat or alcohol is sold anywhere in this town, and its cafes lean vegetarian and Ayurvedic.

sourceName: Common breakfast-stall format, UP-Uttarakhand highway corridor

en.title: A classic kachori-sabzi breakfast is a highway staple here
en.shortDescription: Roadside stalls around Roorkee serve the classic Uttar Pradesh–Uttarakhand breakfast of kachori with spiced potato sabzi, a common quick meal for early travellers on this route.
en.longDescription: Kachori-sabzi — a deep-fried lentil-stuffed kachori served with a spiced potato curry — is a standard roadside breakfast across much of Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand, and stalls around Roorkee are a common stop for travellers making an early start on this corridor.
en.narrationHint: This is classic kachori-sabzi breakfast territory.
